common_name: JaMur Zoysia Grass (Fine-Textured Cold-Hardy Manila Zoysia)

planting.note: Install as sod or plugs once soil is consistently warm in late spring; JaMur is a sterile hybrid and cannot be seeded.

directions: Plant plugs on 6-12 inch centers or lay sod in a full-sun to lightly shaded site, watering daily during the first two to three weeks until roots knit into the soil. JaMur is a Manila-type zoysia selected for a finer leaf blade and denser canopy than older zoysia cultivars while retaining good shade and cold tolerance, making it a popular choice for high-quality residential lawns across the Gulf South. Mow at 1-2 inches with a sharp reel or rotary mower and expect slower establishment and recovery from wear than bermudagrass, since zoysia's dense, wiry growth habit trades speed for long-term durability and a carpet-like texture.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Zoysiagrass for Texas Lawns
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Zoysiagrass in Florida Lawns

common_name: Princess 77 Bermudagrass (Fine-Textured Seeded Hybrid-Type Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Broadcast hulled seed at 1-2 lbs per 1,000 square feet once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F; keep the seedbed consistently moist until germination.

directions: Sow into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late spring and irrigate lightly but frequently until a full stand emerges, then transition to deep, infrequent watering once established. Princess 77 is a seeded bermudagrass bred to approach the fine texture and density of vegetative hybrid cultivars like Tifway while still being propagated economically from seed, giving it a noticeably finer blade than common bermuda. It tolerates heat, drought, and heavy foot traffic well but, like all bermudagrass, needs a minimum of six to eight hours of direct sun daily and will thin quickly in shaded areas.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bermudagrass Varieties for Texas Lawns
Oklahoma State University Extension — Turfgrass Species and Variety Selection

planting.note: Broadcast hulled seed once soil is consistently warm in spring; Yukon establishes readily from seed and does not require sod or plugs.

directions: Prepare a firm, clean seedbed and broadcast seed in late spring, watering lightly several times a day until germination is complete and roots are established. Yukon was bred at Oklahoma State University specifically for winter survival further north than most bermudagrasses, which also translates into unusually early spring green-up and reliable performance across the milder winters of the Gulf Coast. Mow at 1-1.5 inches once established and expect the same full-sun requirement, drought tolerance, and rapid summer growth typical of common bermudagrass.
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension — Bermudagrass Variety Trials
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Warm-Season Turfgrass Variety Comparison

common_name: Latitude 36 Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Fine-Textured Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as sod, sprigs, or plugs from spring through midsummer since Latitude 36 is a sterile hybrid propagated only vegetatively.

directions: Lay sod or plant sprigs in a full-sun site and irrigate consistently for two to three weeks to knit the stand together, then taper to deep, infrequent watering. Latitude 36 is an Oklahoma State University hybrid bermudagrass release prized for combining fine texture and dark color with cold tolerance well beyond typical Gulf Coast hybrids, making it a dependable choice where occasional hard freezes are a concern. It recovers quickly from wear and drought stress once established, but like other hybrid bermudagrasses it needs full sun and a dedicated mowing and fertility program to maintain its dense, fine-bladed appearance.
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivar Development
Sod Solutions — Latitude 36 Bermudagrass Technical Notes

common_name: Oaklawn Centipedegrass (Improved Seeded Low-Maintenance Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Sow a light rate of hulled seed into a weed-free bed in late spring once soil is reliably warm, since centipedegrass seed germinates slowly and unevenly.

directions: Sow lightly, since centipedegrass is easy to overseed, and keep the surface consistently moist for three to four weeks while the slow-growing seedlings establish. Oaklawn is an older selection valued for the same low-input, low-fertility tolerance that makes centipedegrass a favorite lawn choice for gardeners who want to mow and fertilize as little as possible, forming a coarse but dense apple-green sward. Avoid over-liming or over-fertilizing, since centipedegrass is notoriously sensitive to high soil pH and excess nitrogen, both of which can trigger a slow yellowing decline sometimes called centipede decline.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Centipedegrass Lawns

common_name: TifQuik Bahiagrass (Fast-Establishing Seeded Pasture and Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Broadcast seed into a prepared bed in late spring once soil is warm; TifQuik germinates and covers noticeably faster than older bahiagrass cultivars.

directions: Broadcast seed at the recommended pasture or turf rate and keep the top inch of soil moist until a uniform stand emerges, which happens markedly faster than with Argentine or Pensacola bahiagrass. TifQuik is a University of Georgia release bred to shorten the slow, patchy establishment period that has long been bahiagrass's main drawback, making it useful for erosion control and quick cover on Gulf Coast roadsides, pastures, and low-maintenance lawns. Once established it shares bahiagrass's deep taproot, excellent drought tolerance, and open, coarse-bladed growth habit, and needs only occasional mowing to remove its tall seedheads.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Bahiagrass Cultivar Trials
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bahiagrass for Florida Lawns and Pastures
